title: One Hundred Sons Against One
story:
A hundred sons of Shamvara came against Pradyumna at once, on the field before their father's gate, and Krishna's son did not give ground.

They came on as a storm comes, showering him from every side with arrows, spears, axes, javelins, and maces at the same moment, and the field before the gate turned dark with their shafts. Pradyumna, angered, answered each of them with five arrows of his own, and the field rang with bowstrings and the shriek of arrows. The sons of the demon were all good bowmen, and they wove a net of weapons over him to bring him down; Pradyumna cut straight through it. In the first exchanges he killed the ten strongest of the brothers; the next moment, with a broad-headed arrow, he struck Chitrasena down. The last of them, seeing their brothers fall, rushed him together, shooting as they came — and he struck them down one after another, the old text says, as if in sport.

When it was over, all hundred lay on the field. Every one of them had been a good bowman; every one of them was dead. Pradyumna, the pride of Rukmini's heart, stood untouched among the fallen, and the field was quiet except for the wind moving in the fallen flags. He looked toward the city, still wanting battle.

In the palace, the news struck Shamvara like a blow: his hundred sons, gone in a single day. Wrath filled him, and he called for his charioteer, who saluted with his head touching the ground, brought the king's war-car, and roused the soldiers to readiness. It was a dreadful thing to see — drawn by a thousand bears and lashed with ropes of serpents, armored in tiger skin, hung with nets of small bells and painted over with stars, its flags worked with golden lions, tall as the summit of a mountain, with gold flashing from every standard. Shamvara put on golden armor, took up his bow and arrows, and set out as though something were driving him, with his four ministers — Durdhara, Ketumali, Shatruhanta, and Pramardana — around him and his army spread across the plain behind: two hundred chariots, ten thousand elephants, eight thousand horses, and foot soldiers beyond counting, ten lakh of them, a lakh being a hundred thousand.

The sky itself seemed to turn against the march. Cranes screamed overhead; firebrands fell among the columns; jackals howled at the army; vultures settled on the tops of the standards. The moon was eclipsed and ringed with shadow; his left eye and his left arm trembled of their own accord; the horses' pace slackened by itself; and Indra sent down a shower of blood mixed with live coals and cinders, until the reins slipped from the charioteer's hands.

Shamvara paid no attention to any of it. Rage had closed his eyes to omens. He drove on, bent on slaying Pradyumna, and the earth shook under the sound of bugles, conch shells, and drums blown together; beasts and birds fled in terror from the noise.

On the far side of the field, Krishna's son stood alone among the fallen, and he too was bent on slaying his enemy. He watched the horizon darken with the dust of an army, and at its head the monstrous chariot drawn by bears. He had called the demon out, and the demon was coming — and the boy who had mastered every form of illusion stood his ground and waited.
reflection: The omens read the end before the battle begins — the eclipse, the vultures, the blood falling from a clear sky — and only Shamvara refuses to see them. Rage, the text suggests, is the one blindness no seer can cure.
content_note: Battle violence: Pradyumna kills the hundred sons of Shamvara in a single fight; the deaths are recounted without graphic detail.
next_story_tease: The father himself was coming — and he did not come alone.
hero_scene: The battlefield strewn with the fallen hundred; Pradyumna standing alone amid the wreck of bows and standards, bow in hand, as the horizon darkens with the dust of Shamvara's monstrous bear-drawn chariot and his army.
